bio: Cory Anthony Booker (born April 27, 1969) is an American politician currently serving as the junior United States Senator from New Jersey, in office since 2013. The first African-American U.S. Senator from New Jersey, he was previously the 36th Mayor of Newark from 2006 to 2013. ground_truth: Asian and Latino and black and white, Christian, Hindu, Sikh, Americans, literally guys with kippahs on, Jews with kippahs on, cheering Muslims as they came out of the airport, cheering them. That was one of the most proudest moments I've had as an American, where I saw our country's truth, where people came out of their homes to be there for someone else who they didn't even know, who might not even have been an American citizen. That's the love. That's the principles. Those are the ideals that we're about. And so that family in Redding, Pennsylvania, that has a Trump sign in their yard, they are my neighbor. They are my fellow citizen. I will not hate you. I will not look down on you. I will not undermine the truth of who you are, that you have dignity and you want for your family and your children what I want. Yes, in the civic space, we have to have arguments and debates, but if we descend into a country that has no ability... No ability for courageous empathy or to call to the moral imagination of this country, if that's where we end up, then we're never going to get to where we need to go, a society that values us all and begins to help to break through the veils that separate us to the truth that the only way this country is going to thrive is if the people who we stuff in our prisons or the people who we have that are stuck in dead-end jobs, living below the poverty line, even though they work 40, 50 hours a week, the only way we get to a point where we love and have... A sense of urgency about their condition is if we stop vilifying each other and see each other for who we are. And I'll end with this. Ralph Ellison wrote this book, The Invisible Man, and you know from your own life what it feels like to be seen as less than human or to be seen as without your dignity. This is the problem right now. One of my greatest heroes in Newark, a tenant organizer, you'll never know his name, but he's responsible for thousands of people having a roof over their head. So many cities are there, you know, tenants who are forced to cram into the widows' rooms. And it's not real. It's not real. people there to see him, crowded rooms, but I realized that for this guy it's not about popularity, it's about purpose, it's not about celebrity, it's about significance. And his last words to me were, I love you. And that's the message. I see you. I love you. I see you. I love you. If we as Americans could begin to see each other and love each other and work and understand that I may be, hey, I may be making it in America, but I'm not making it if my neighbor isn't. I'm not making it if a family's worrying about their health care or worrying about how they're going to put food on the table or living in an environmentally savage community. We could start really seeing each other and understanding the truth that we are one people, e pluribus unum, with one destiny, that we need each other, that we belong to each other. If we can get to that point and understand that the lines that divide us are nowhere near the ties that bind us, that's when America will ascend and continue to be a light unto day.
